content: The Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure was introduced into the London Guidelines in 1989. Its primary objectives were to assist importing countries in understanding the potential hazards of chemicals being shipped to them, to establish a decision-making process for future imports, and to encourage exporting countries to take measures to prevent the export of unwanted pesticides. In 1998, the PIC procedure was formalized into a legally binding agreement known as the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade. This Convention came into effect in 2004 and applies to both pesticides and industrial chemicals. While it includes some obligations related to domestic production and use, its main focus is on the import and export of chemicals. The PIC procedure serves as a mechanism to formally obtain and disseminate decisions made by importing countries regarding hazardous chemicals. Chemicals listed in Annex III of the Convention can only be exported in accordance with the importing country’s decision. The overarching goal is to protect human health and the environment by facilitating the exchange of information about hazardous chemicals, including pesticides, and enabling countries to make informed decisions about their import and export. Once a chemical is listed in Annex III, all parties to the Rotterdam Convention are required to implement the PIC procedure for that chemical. Parties must also establish appropriate legislative and administrative measures to ensure compliance with import and export obligations under the Convention. These measures must not be more restrictive for imports than those applied to domestically produced goods. The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), which entered into force in 2004, aims to eliminate the production and use of chemicals classified as POPs. These are organic compounds that persist in the environment, accumulate in the fatty tissues of living organisms, and are toxic to humans and wildlife. POPs are particularly dangerous due to their long-term effects, even though these effects may not be immediately apparent. The Convention categorizes chemicals into three lists: Annex A for chemicals to be eliminated, Annex B for chemicals to be restricted, and Annex C for chemicals that are unintentional by-products of certain production processes and must be reduced. The most up-to-date list of these chemicals is available on the Convention’s website. Many of these chemicals are also listed under the Rotterdam Convention. Article 3 of the Stockholm Convention outlines detailed prohibitions on Annex A chemicals and specifies the obligations of contracting parties to eliminate their production, use, import, and export. It also sets restrictions on the production and use of Annex B chemicals. Imports of chemicals for environmentally sound disposal are exempted, as are specific production and use exemptions for chemicals listed in both Annex A and B, such as those used for disease vector control under certain conditions. Parties to the Convention are required to prohibit the production and use of most listed chemicals under Annexes A and B at the national level. The Convention also establishes requirements for the management of POP stockpiles and wastes. The Basel Convention on the Transboundary Movement of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, which came into force in 1992, regulates the international shipment of hazardous wastes. Although not specifically focused on pesticides, it addresses obsolete pesticides and substances that may be by-products or waste products from pesticides. This Convention is particularly useful for national governments seeking to prevent the dumping of waste products, such as obsolete pesticides, within their borders, especially in cases where governments lack the capacity to manage these wastes in an environmentally sound manner. The Basel Convention targets hazardous wastes, which are defined as those belonging to any category listed in Annex I and exhibiting one or more characteristics outlined in Annex III. Annex I includes wastes from the production, formulation, and use of biocides (pesticides). The Convention applies particularly to obsolete pesticide stocks requiring disposal. Under the Basel Convention, state parties may prohibit the import of hazardous wastes or specific types of hazardous wastes. Exporting states may only move hazardous wastes across borders after providing prior written notification to the importing state and receiving written consent. While the Convention has primarily focused on the transboundary movement of wastes, it also imposes obligations relevant to the development of national legislation, such as ensuring the availability of adequate disposal facilities, establishing criminal penalties for violations, and requiring proper labeling, packaging, and documentation for hazardous wastes in shipment. The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer addresses one specific pesticide, methyl bromide, which depletes the ozone layer. Industrialized countries were required to eliminate the production of methyl bromide by January 2005, with certain exceptions for pre-shipment, quarantine, emergency uses, and critical uses authorized under the Protocol. Developing countries were given a grace period but have agreed to phase out methyl bromide on a faster timetable. These exemptions are intended to be temporary and strictly limited. Several International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions address the safety and health of workers exposed to chemicals in the workplace, particularly in agriculture. The C184 Safety and Health in Agriculture Convention, adopted in 2001 and effective in 2003, specifically addresses the safety and health of agricultural workers exposed to pesticides. However, many agricultural workers, especially informal laborers, are not covered by occupational health and safety legislation. ILO Convention No. 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour, adopted in 1999, identifies work that is likely to harm the health, safety, or morals of children as a worst form of child labor. This includes the application of pesticides, given children’s increased vulnerability to the toxic effects of many pesticides. The Agriculture Convention imposes responsibilities on employers, strengthens the rights of agricultural workers, and places obligations on governments to develop coherent national policies on safety and health in agriculture, consult employers and trade unions, establish responsible authorities, and ensure inspection systems. The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) aims to eliminate chemical weapons by prohibiting their development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, retention, transfer, or use. State parties are required to destroy any stockpiles of chemical weapons and production facilities they may hold. The CWC also establishes a verification regime for certain toxic chemicals and their precursors to ensure they are only used for non-prohibited purposes. Some pesticides may be chemically related to compounds listed in the CWC, which could have implications for their production, importation, and storage. Non-binding international instruments, often referred to as soft law, include plans of action, declarations, codes of conduct, guidelines, and technical standards. These instruments promote international harmonization and are often developed by experts. While not legally binding, they have significantly influenced national pesticide legislation. The Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, originally adopted in 1985 and subsequently revised, provides a reference framework for governments, the pesticide industry, and other stakeholders. It is supported by technical guidelines that offer detailed guidance on specific aspects of the pesticide life cycle. The Code of Conduct is voluntary but widely used to shape pesticide legislation. The Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC), a joint body of FAO and WHO, develops harmonized food standards, including maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides. These MRLs are established by the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues (CCPR) and are recognized by the WTO. Some governments have adopted Codex MRLs as legally binding standards to ensure compliance with international consensus. The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) is an internationally agreed tool for chemical hazard communication. It incorporates harmonized hazard classification criteria and provisions for standardized label information and safety data sheets (SDSs). GHS covers all chemicals, including pesticides, and aims to ensure that information on chemical hazards is available to workers and consumers in a harmonized format. GHS classification replaces the WHO Classification of Pesticides by Hazard, adding chronic human toxicity and environmental toxicity to acute human toxicity, making it more comprehensive. An increasing number of countries are adopting GHS classification as a binding standard through national legislation.
